title: Design secure network architectures and segmentation: concept decisions 1
teachingQuestion: Which boundary, protocol endpoint, and management path constrain a risky flow without creating an unseen bypass?
focalInsight: Security comes from matched physical, logical, workload, identity, and observable enforcement—not from a topology label or encryption alone.
caption: Read across a row to connect meaning, decision and consequence. Use the retrieval answer to check your explanation after reading the linked scenario.

nodes.label: Osi Model
nodes.definition: Seven-layer reference model for locating communication functions, controls, and faults.
nodes.detail: Seven-layer reference model for locating communication functions, controls, and faults.
nodes.decision: Use it to locate the affected function and control, while recognizing real protocols can span layers.
nodes.failureExample: Calling an application authorization flaw a Layer 3 issue directs remediation to routing.
nodes.retrievalAnswer: Use OSI to name the layer/function before choosing a control.

nodes.label: Tcp Ip Model
nodes.definition: Implementation-oriented stack that groups networking functions into fewer protocol layers.
nodes.detail: Implementation-oriented stack that groups networking functions into fewer protocol layers.
nodes.decision: Use it to reason about deployed Internet protocols; translate, rather than equate blindly, to OSI terms.
nodes.failureExample: Assuming TCP/IP and OSI layers map one-for-one obscures where encryption or routing terminates.
nodes.retrievalAnswer: TCP/IP is a deployed stack; OSI is a comparison vocabulary.

nodes.label: Traffic Flows
nodes.definition: Documented north-south and east-west communications among users, services, management, and dependencies.
nodes.detail: Documented north-south and east-west communications among users, services, management, and dependencies.
nodes.decision: Allow only flows with known purpose, source/destination identity, protocol, path, and monitoring point.
nodes.failureExample: An undocumented east-west path lets a compromised workload reach a sensitive service.
nodes.retrievalAnswer: A flow record needs endpoints, purpose, enforcement point, and evidence.

nodes.label: Network Planes
nodes.definition: Data plane forwards traffic; control plane decides forwarding; management plane configures and administers devices.
nodes.detail: Data plane forwards traffic; control plane decides forwarding; management plane configures and administers devices.
nodes.decision: Separate and protect planes where risk warrants, especially management identities and control interfaces.
nodes.failureExample: A protected data path still fails if an attacker reconfigures it through the management plane.
nodes.retrievalAnswer: Name the plane an attacker would target to change routes.

nodes.label: Network Observability
nodes.definition: Flow, fault, capacity, and policy telemetry that lets operators detect and explain network behavior.
nodes.detail: Flow, fault, capacity, and policy telemetry that lets operators detect and explain network behavior.
nodes.decision: Collect protected, actionable signals at enforcement and management points without creating an unmanaged collector path.
nodes.failureExample: Encryption or segmentation failures remain invisible when denied flows and device health are not observed.
nodes.retrievalAnswer: Observability must show policy outcome and device/flow health.

nodes.label: Secure Protocols
nodes.definition: Protocols selected for a specific layer, endpoint identity, confidentiality, integrity, and failure model.
nodes.detail: Protocols selected for a specific layer, endpoint identity, confidentiality, integrity, and failure model.
nodes.decision: Choose by protected traffic, termination points, key/certificate validation, metadata exposure, inspection, and availability impact.
nodes.failureExample: Selecting “encryption” without locating endpoints leaves an onward path unprotected.
nodes.retrievalAnswer: Ask where protection terminates and what remains exposed.

nodes.label: Wireless Security
nodes.definition: Controls for radio association, encryption, admission, rogue detection, management, and RF availability.
nodes.detail: Controls for radio association, encryption, admission, rogue detection, management, and RF availability.
nodes.decision: Match authentication, segmentation, monitoring, and physical/radio risks to the wireless use case.
nodes.failureExample: A strong Wi-Fi password does not isolate guest or IoT traffic from enterprise services.
nodes.retrievalAnswer: Wireless security includes admission, segmentation, and rogue/association monitoring.

nodes.label: Software Defined Networking
nodes.definition: Architecture that separates/centralizes programmable network control from forwarding devices through software control interfaces.
nodes.detail: Architecture that separates/centralizes programmable network control from forwarding devices through software control interfaces.
nodes.decision: Protect controller identity, policy changes, APIs, availability, logs, and rollback as a high-value control plane.
nodes.failureExample: A compromised SDN controller can alter policy across many forwarding devices.
nodes.retrievalAnswer: In SDN, the controller/control API is a critical trust boundary.

nodes.label: Micro Segmentation
nodes.definition: Fine-grained workload or identity-aware policy enforced close to services rather than only at large network zones.
nodes.detail: Fine-grained workload or identity-aware policy enforced close to services rather than only at large network zones.
nodes.decision: Use when east-west blast radius matters and maintain explicit service identity, policy, and observability.
nodes.failureExample: A broad subnet rule lets one compromised host laterally reach every workload in the segment.
nodes.retrievalAnswer: Micro-segmentation asks which workload may call which service.
